# Capability Threat Model

This is the one page that says what March's capability system protects against, what it
assumes, and what it does not do. Three older pages each describe a part of it, and before
2026-10-30 they disagreed with each other:

- [Capabilities]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/capabilities/) is the language feature (`needs`,
  `Cap(X)`, the upper limit, `main`'s grant).
- [Capability Enforcement]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/capability-enforcement/) covers the OS
  sandbox (`--cap-sandbox`, `forge cap run`) and the hot-deploy admission gate.
- [Capability Audit]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/capability-audit/) covers `forge audit` and
  `forge cap inspect`.
- The design history is in
  [`specs/2026-08-04-provable-sandbox-design.md`](https://github.com/march-language/march/blob/main/specs/2026-08-04-provable-sandbox-design.md).

Where this page and one of those disagree, this page is the one checked against the code,
and the other is a bug to fix. Every behaviour below was checked against the compiler
on 2026-10-30. The [capabilities claim]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/claim-capabilities/) is the
short version of this page.

## Who the attacker is

The system is built for one situation: **you run code you did not write line by line**,
mostly your dependencies, and want to know and limit what it can touch.

| Party | Trusted? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| You, writing the program and choosing `main`'s grant | Yes | You decide the policy. |
| The March compiler, runtime and standard library | Yes | They do the checking. A bug in them is a bug in the claim (see [Assumptions](#assumptions)). |
| Your dependencies (March source) | **No** | This is the main case. A dependency can be careless or hostile. |
| C code reached through `extern` | **No, and not analysed** | The compiler can't see inside it. See [`IO.Foreign`](#foreign-code-ioforeign). |
| Whoever signs a hot deploy | Partly | The node checks the signature and a policy, but it trusts the patch's own list of capabilities. See [Hot deploys](#hot-deploys). |
| Someone with a shell on the machine | **No, and out of scope** | They can run the binary under a debugger or swap it. |

## What is checked, layer by layer

### 1. At compile time, always on

These checks run on every `march --check` and `march --compile`. There is no flag to skip
the first three.

**Every module declares what it touches (`needs`).** If any function in a module reaches a
capability the module does not declare in `needs`, the build fails with
[`cap_needs`]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/errors/cap_needs/). This holds for every route:
a `Cap(X)` in a signature, a capability builtin called directly (`file_write(...)`), and a
function from another module that needs it. It is an error, not a warning, and it fires
even for a function nothing calls. (Calling a builtin directly was only a warning before
2026-08-06. Some older pages still said so; they were wrong after that date.)

**The upper limit (the "ceiling").** The compiler checks every module's *emitted* code,
after inlining and specialisation, against that module's own `needs`, and fails the build
(`[cap_ceiling]`) if a module uses a
capability it did not declare, including through a standard-library wrapper such as
`File.write`. This covers dependencies that never opted into anything. It is on by
default; `--no-cap-strict` turns off the emitted-code part (the `needs` check above still
runs). `march --compile` runs the full check; `march --check` runs a subset of it that
doesn't over-report.

**`main`'s grant bounds the whole program.** `main`'s capability parameters are the
program's grant. A program that reaches anything outside the grant fails to build
(`[cap_grant_exceeded]`), no matter
what any module declares. A `main` with no capability parameter is granted nothing, so a
program that performs IO without stating its grant does not compile
([`cap_grant`]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/errors/cap_grant/)). `Cap(IO)` grants everything.
Code that is never reached from `main` costs nothing against the grant.

**Capabilities can't be forged or widened.** A `Cap(X)` value can only be received (from
`main`, or from a function that was given it) and narrowed to something smaller
(`cap_narrow`). It can't be built from JSON, a literal or any other data, and it can't be
widened. Proof capabilities (`Session.Live`, your own `proof cap`) can only be created by
the module that declares them.

**Per-role grants.** A protocol role declared `role Ledger needs IO.FileWrite` gets its
grant checked the same way `main`'s is: its code may reach only what the role names.

### 2. What is *not* checked per function

There are **no per-function capability bounds** in 1.0 today. Inside a module, every
function shares that module's `needs`. A `Cap(X)` parameter marks authority at a module
boundary, but it does not limit what that function reaches.

A per-function check did exist from 2026-08-10 to 2026-08-13 ("R1 stage C", a check
called `check_fn_grants`). It was removed on 2026-08-13 because it forced every caller to
pass capabilities it didn't otherwise need
([`specs/progress/2026-08-13-remove-per-function-grant-ceiling.md`](https://github.com/march-language/march/blob/main/specs/progress/2026-08-13-remove-per-function-grant-ceiling.md)).
The provable-sandbox design page described it as shipped; that was true for those three
days only.

A declared per-function bound with no effect on callers (`fn fetch(url) needs
IO.NetConnect.TLS do`) is **planned** for 1.0, with module-level bounds as the fallback if
it proves too noisy (road-to-1.0 plan, "Pillar 2 — per-function bounds"). The per-function
data it needs already exists (`lib/caps/cap_rows.ml`); only the declaration and the check
are missing.

### 3. Reading a binary or a dependency tree

Two tools report what code may do. They do not stop it.

- **`forge audit`** compares your dependencies' capabilities with a recorded baseline
  (`forge.caps.lock`) and exits 1 when one asks for more. `forge add`, `forge deps` and
  `forge outdated` run the same comparison. By default it reads `needs` declarations,
  which the compile-time checks above keep honest; `--inferred` reads what the code uses.
- **`forge cap inspect <binary>`** reads the capability markers and runtime symbols left
  in a compiled binary, says which module is responsible for each, and with `--strict`
  re-checks the upper limit on a binary you didn't build.

### 4. At run time, opt-in: the OS sandbox

Everything above is checked before the program runs and then erased. To make the
operating system enforce the grant on the running process, which also covers C code and
raw syscalls, you opt in:

- **`march --compile --cap-sandbox`**: the binary installs a deny-by-default sandbox on
  itself before any of your code runs (Seatbelt on macOS, seccomp-bpf on Linux). It
  **fails closed**: if the sandbox can't be installed, or the platform or CPU architecture
  isn't supported, the program exits (status 70) instead of running unconfined.
  **Decided 2026-10-30: it stays opt-in in 1.0, and keeps failing closed.**
- **`forge cap run [--allow-only X] ./binary`**: forge puts the sandbox on from outside
  before the program starts (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux). With `--allow-only`
  you choose the policy, so a binary that under-reports its capabilities gains nothing.

Not every capability can be enforced by every OS mechanism. The ones that can't are
reported as **advisory**, never silently dropped. In short: `IO.FileRead` is advisory under
`--cap-sandbox` on both platforms (enforced by `forge cap run` on Linux); `IO.NetListen` is
advisory under `forge cap run` on Linux; `IO.Clock`, `IO.Spawn`, `IO.Console`, `IO.Random`
and `IO.Foreign` are advisory everywhere. The full table, capability by capability, is on
[Capability Enforcement]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/capability-enforcement/#os-primitives-capability-by-capability).

The sandbox works on tier-1 platforms only (darwin-arm64, linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64;
see [Supported Platforms]({{ site.baseurl }}/docs/platforms/)).

### 5. Hot deploys

A hot deploy (`forge deploy hot`) replaces functions in a running program. It has two
gates:

- **On your machine**, a deploy that widens what a function or protocol role may reach
  stops unless you pass `--grant-cap` for the new capabilities.
- **On the node**, each activated function arrives signed (ed25519) with its own list of
  capabilities and a BLAKE3 digest of that list. The node rejects a tampered list, and,
  if `MARCH_DEPLOY_POLICY` names a policy file, rejects a function or role whose
  capabilities fall outside it.

The node gate trusts the patch's *own* list: anyone with the signing key can claim less
than the code uses. With no `MARCH_DEPLOY_POLICY` set, every signed patch is admitted.
**A hot deploy is therefore outside the "the grant bounds the program" claim.** Under
`--cap-sandbox` the OS sandbox installed at startup still applies to patched code, because
it can't be loosened at run time.

## Foreign code (`IO.Foreign`)

An `extern` block calls C, and the compiler's knowledge stops there. The rules:

- A module with an `extern` block should declare `needs IO.Foreign`. If it doesn't, the
  compiler warns (`[extern_needs_foreign]`).
  This is still a warning, not an error.
- A program that reaches an `extern` block can't be built under any grant narrower than
  `Cap(IO)`: a narrow grant over C code would be a lie, so the compiler refuses it.
- `forge audit` and `forge cap inspect` report `IO.Foreign`; read it as "the rest of this
  list is no longer complete".

So the compile-time claim covers March code only. For C code, the OS sandbox is the only
enforcement.

## Assumptions

The compile-time claim holds only if all of these are true:

1. **The compiler, runtime and standard library are correct.** The checks are a
   whole-program static analysis, not a proof. No machine-checked proof covers them (the
   Lean model of the type system has no grant check).
2. **Every language form is visited by the capability walks.** The checks follow a static
   reference graph. A new language form the walk forgets is a hole: five past bugs were
   exactly that. Nothing tests this mechanically yet (see [Gates](#gates)).
3. **You build with the default checks on.** `--no-cap-strict` drops the emitted-code
   check.
4. **The binary you run is the one you built.** Nothing stops someone from replacing it
   after the build. Release archives are checksummed but not yet signed.
5. **No C code, or C code you trust.** See [Foreign code](#foreign-code-ioforeign).

## What is not claimed

- **Per-function bounds.** A module's functions share its authority (see
  [above](#2-what-is-not-checked-per-function)).
- **What code does with a capability it holds.** `IO.NetConnect` allows a telemetry ping
  and a data leak equally.
- **Output to the console.** Anything a program may print, it may leak; no capability
  stops that.
- **C code, `dlopen` and raw syscalls**, unless you run under the OS sandbox.
- **Hot-patched code beyond its signed, self-reported list** (see [Hot deploys](#5-hot-deploys)).
- **Against whoever builds the binary.** `--cap-sandbox` is chosen by the person
  compiling, so a hostile publisher simply leaves it out. For code you don't trust, use
  `forge cap run --allow-only`.
- **Capabilities the OS can't tell apart** (the advisory rows above).

## Known holes (open today)

- **Path scopes.** `needs IO.FileWrite("/var/lib/app")` narrows the sandbox, but a few
  calls can bypass the compile-time scope check
  ([`specs/todos/2026-08-04-path-scope-followups.md`](https://github.com/march-language/march/blob/main/specs/todos/2026-08-04-path-scope-followups.md)).
- **The reload server under `--cap-sandbox`.** A deploy's own file writes happen under a
  withheld `IO.FileWrite`
  ([`specs/todos/2026-10-18-hcr-reload-writes-under-cap-sandbox.md`](https://github.com/march-language/march/blob/main/specs/todos/2026-10-18-hcr-reload-writes-under-cap-sandbox.md)).
- **Handles minted from a name.** `Vault.open(name)` and `Vault.whereis(name)` turn any
  string into a handle whose element type the caller chooses (`stdlib/vault.march`). This
  is a type-safety gap rather than an authority gap, but it is the same pattern a
  capability must never follow.

## Gates

What runs in CI today:

- The capability unit tests in the `run_compiler` suite (`test/test_cap_*.ml`, including
  the ceiling, unforgeability and both sandbox tests), on Linux (`test (ubuntu, compiler)`)
  and macOS (`test (macos-15, all)`).
- The capability rejects in the static-semantics corpus (`specs/lang/types/reject/`), run by
  the `conformance` job.
- `--cap-sandbox` runs real compiled binaries and checks that withheld operations fail
  (`test/test_cap_sandbox_runtime.ml`).

**Planned, not built:**

- A **walk-completeness test**: every syntax-tree and IR constructor is visited by every
  capability walk, checked mechanically instead of by review.
- A **must-reject corpus**: one program per past capability bypass, run in CI.
- The Lean model of the type system has no grant check, so it can't catch a grant bug.
